title: Introducing the Legora BAR — The Legora Benchmark for Agentic Reasoning
author: Jacob Lauritzen · Emil Sjölander · Ebba Helfer · Firas Danil

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: Legora accepts the cluster’s core distinction between headline quality scores and dependable complete-task performance, then materially extends it with risk-weighted scoring that heavily penalizes consequential omissions. It also shows that model performance diverges as legal work becomes longer and more complex, reinforcing task-specific rather than general capability claims.
qs: Since high-importance misses are penalized heavily, a materially incomplete deliverable still scores like one.
The models perform similarly on shorter legal work and begin to show variance as the work gets longer and more complex, where sustaining judgment across a full matter is critical.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: Legora accepts the cluster’s core demand for realistic, task-specific legal-AI evaluation and materially extends it by testing end-to-end work within the deployed system—including its harness and tools—rather than treating the model name as the unit of performance. Its risk-weighted rubric also directly addresses the cluster’s concern that partial credit can obscure consequential omissions. However, BAR’s private cases and vendor-run judging limit independent reproducibility, so its reported results remain system-specific evidence rather than proof of general production competence.
qs: Legora BAR evaluates AI models across a comprehensive set of end-to-end legal tasks drawn from real-world cases, purpose-built to track how Legora performs as both the underlying models and our own harness advance over time.
Since high-importance misses are penalized heavily, a materially incomplete deliverable still scores like one.

st.t: Legal quality: Scoring methods encode different harms
st.an: Legora supports the cluster’s proposition that scoring methods encode different conceptions of consequential legal error. It argues that importance-weighted rubrics preserve distinctions between minor and material omissions that all-or-nothing completion obscures. Its methodology and worked example illustrate that position, but do not comparatively validate the weighting scheme or the reliability and robustness of its LLM judge.
qs: All-or-nothing grading collapses every result into a single pass/fail and hides where systems actually differ, on the hard work where the differences matter most.

Weighted scoring mirrors how a partner reviews work: omitting a defined term and omitting a material change-of-control provision are both drafting errors, but no partner treats them as equally serious.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s narrower claim that capability and performance vary by task difficulty and that evaluation should consider multiple deployment-relevant dimensions, including quality, latency and cost. Its benchmark evidence is limited to model comparisons and does not independently address user expertise, verification, workflow redesign or realised organisational value.

kp.k: Benchmarking targets complete legal systems rather than isolated models
kp.d: Legora argues that legal AI quality depends on the model, harness, tools and operating environment together. BAR evaluates end-to-end legal tasks inside the same Legora harness and aOS used by customers, which the company presents as more representative of practical experience than synthetic environments with simplified benchmarking harnesses.
qs: The quality of a legal AI product is about more than the underlying model. It's the combination of the model, the harness, the tools it has access to, and the system it operates within.
Our benchmark evaluates models on real legal cases across practice areas, inside the Legora harness and the Legora aOS™.

kp.k: BAR samples a larger professionally reviewed legal task corpus
kp.d: Legora reports a corpus of 5,161 cases across 28 practice areas containing 11,075 source documents, with each case reviewed by a legal professional. BAR itself comprises hundreds of cases drafted by law firm partners and in-house legal engineers, rather than the entire corpus. Legora describes the subset as representative of the full suite's practice areas, task types and difficulty levels.
qs: We maintain a growing evaluation corpus of over 5,000 cases across 28 practice areas (see below), each reviewed by a legal professional.
The Legora BAR is a carefully selected subset made up of hundreds of cases drafted by our law firm partners and in-house legal engineers.
**Cases: 5,161** — Each a complete task set inside a real matter, graded case by case.
**Source Documents: 11,075** — The files that make up the cases, from source material to precedents and prior drafts.

kp.k: Task difficulty reflects estimated senior-associate effort
kp.d: The benchmark categorizes tasks by the time a legal expert would require, not by measured AI time savings. Short tasks require a few hours up to approximately half a day; medium tasks one to three days; long tasks a week or more, up to hundreds of hours. These range from discrete reviews to complete pleadings, position papers and deal document sets requiring sustained senior judgment.
qs: Therefore, we added the difficulty dimension to our benchmark, where its definition is rooted in something very familiar to legal professionals: how much time the work would take a legal expert.
| Short | A few hours, up to ~half a day | A bounded, well-specified piece of work: a discrete question, a single document checked against a few points. |
| Medium | One to three days | A complete work product an associate would be assigned: a memo, a redline against a playbook, a pleaded section, a disclosure schedule. |

| Long | A week or more, up to hundreds of hours | An end-to-end delivery that moves the whole matter forward: a full position paper, a complete pleading, a deal's document set. Sustained senior judgment across a large, messy record. |

kp.k: Private cases protect know-how and address training contamination
kp.d: Legora says partner use cases contain synthesized and/or anonymized data but retain participant know-how and intellectual property, preventing open publication. It also argues that keeping cases private prevents scores from reflecting prior training exposure. One fully synthetic case, co-created with AfterQuery, is public; the document reports AfterQuery's review of that case and the data-curation methodology.
qs: The benchmark runs on real law firm use cases supplied by recognized partners with synthesized and/or anonymized data.
As we use real know-how and IP from participants, we do not open-source them.
When benchmark cases are made public, they end up in the training data of the next model generation.
AfterQuery reviewed it to confirm our data-curation methodology meets industry standards.

kp.k: Lawyers define quality criteria; an LLM scores outputs
kp.d: Cases combine a workflow prompt, matter file room, Legora deliverable and expert-written binary rubrics covering facts, analysis, citations and recommendations. Evaluations run in isolated platform sandboxes, with each case repeated three consecutive times for every model and scored by an LLM judge against the rubrics. Legora says the repetitions ensure statistical relevance and states that a fuller technical account will follow.
qs: They are expert-written, binary, individually verifiable criteria covering facts, analysis, citations, and recommendations.
We run our evaluations in isolated sandbox environments within the Legora platform.
Each case is run three consecutive times to ensure statistical relevance, and the output gets scored by an LLM-as-a-judge, which then gets compared to the corresponding rubrics.
A more in-depth blog post on the technical set-up of our evaluation platform will follow shortly.

kp.k: Risk-weighted rubrics distinguish material errors from minor omissions
kp.d: Legora rejects all-or-nothing grading in favor of a weighted Quality Rubric Score. Legal engineers classify criteria as high, medium or low importance according to stakeholder risk, so material omissions reduce scores more heavily. The agreement-review example scores 90% despite missing a low-importance secondary filing deadline; this is an illustration of scoring, not an aggregate benchmark result.
qs: All-or-nothing grading collapses every result into a single pass/fail and hides where systems actually differ, on the hard work where the differences matter most.
They draw knowledge from their expertise, and mark rubrics as high/medium/low importance dependent on how much risk the deliverable exposes its stakeholders to if the rubric was not met.

kp.k: Reported model differences widen on longer legal workflows
kp.d: Legora reports similar performance on short work and greater variation as tasks become longer and more complex. Its narrative identifies Fable 5, Grok 4.5, Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 as significantly above average on the longest tasks. These are vendor-reported comparisons within the Legora harness. The supplied chart description gives relative normalization and labels rather than underlying numeric scores; it describes seven models while listing eight series.
qs: The models perform similarly on shorter legal work and begin to show variance as the work gets longer and more complex, where sustaining judgment across a full matter is critical.
On the longest running tasks, Fable 5, Grok 4.5, Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 all significantly outperform the average across the full suite.
**Quality by difficulty** (each difficulty panel normalized to the average of the seven shown models within that difficulty; axis gridlines 0.75× / 1.00× / 1.10× / 1.25×).

kp.k: Model selection balances quality, speed and operating cost
kp.d: Legora argues that output quality alone is insufficient for model selection: repetitive short tasks and bulk Tabular Review may prioritize speed and cost. It reports Grok 4.5 as having the lowest time per case with high quality, and Grok 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8 as offering high quality at below-average cost. Cost comparisons use public list prices per case, not client legal fees.
qs: For repetitive short tasks, or bulk operations in Tabular Review, speed and cost might be the key metrics legal teams might optimize for.
When we look at the trade-off between quality and speed, we see a spread across the model set with Grok 4.5 showing up with lowest time per case, at a high quality output.
On Quality vs. Cost, models like Grok 4.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 deliver high quality and lower cost compared to the average of the set.
(Average cost per case at public list prices.)

kp.k: Harness changes reportedly improved quality without changing models
kp.d: Legora attributes an approximately 5% average relative quality uplift between June and July 2026 to harness and platform improvements, comparing the same models across both months. It reports a 5% increase across models live in production and explicitly says the chart shows direction and approximate scale rather than absolute scores.
qs: Since launching the Legora aOS, we have used the BAR results to improve our harness, delivering a 5% increase in relative output quality across all models that are live in production.
Because the models themselves did not change, the uplift reflects advances in the Legora harness and platform rather than in any individual model.
The chart shows direction and approximate scale, not absolute scores.
(≈ +5% average uplift, June 2026 → July 2026.)

kp.k: Citation metrics support lawyers' ability to check answers
kp.d: Legora presents source transparency as necessary for trust and lawyers' fact-checking. Its Cited Answers metric measures whether each claim has a citation; Grounding measures whether consulted sources are reflected in citations. These are the stated benchmark definitions, not reported human verification outcomes. Legora reports OpenAI models highest on Cited Answers and Fable 5 and Opus 4.8 particularly strong on Grounding.
qs: Lawyers must have the ability to fact check every answer Legora produces, which is why we back all of our answers with citations.
The **Cited Answers** score checks whether each claim carries a citation at all.
The **Grounding** score checks whether the source documents the AI consulted to generate an answer, are reflected in the citations.
In the chart below we see that OpenAI models rank highest in Cited Answers scores. On the Grounding Scores, Fable 5 and Opus 4.8 show up particularly strong.

kp.k: Expected deliverables retain explicit escalation of unsupported issues
kp.d: The example tasks specify substantive drafting and review while reserving unresolved issues for human decisions. NDA review should identify out-of-policy positions and decision points; litigation drafting should exclude unsupported claims; transfer-pricing drafting should flag record inconsistencies for confirmation. These are benchmark expectations, not evidence that every evaluated model meets them.
qs: A short cover note listing only the points that need a decision.
Claims the record cannot support are left out rather than pleaded and hedged.
Known inconsistencies in the record are flagged and routed for confirmation rather than silently resolved.

kp.k: Continuous evaluation directs development toward harder agentic matters
kp.d: Legora describes BAR as a continuous product-development feedback loop rather than a one-off comparison. It says the corpus grows monthly, fastest in full end-to-end matters, and asserts that agents are only now capable enough for measurement on these hardest cases to be meaningful.
qs: We run the benchmark continuously: every evaluation helps our team identify where to improve next, and each improvement ships directly into the Legora platform.
The benchmark corpus grows every month, with the fastest growth in the hardest cases: full end-to-end matters where agents are only now capable enough for the measurement to mean something.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Legora Research claims that agentic AI is becoming capable of undertaking complex, end-to-end legal workflows, including work requiring sustained senior judgment.
pts.d: Jacob Lauritzen, Emil Sjölander, Ebba Helfer and Firas Danil describe agents producing matter-level deliverables rather than only answering discrete questions. Examples include NDA redlines, arbitration pleadings and a transfer-pricing Master File. They say agents are only now sufficiently capable for measurement on the hardest matters to be meaningful. The senior-associate effort categories describe the human work represented by tasks, not demonstrated hours saved or a claim that lawyers can be replaced.

pts.k: The authors claim that legal-AI quality depends on the complete operating system, not just the underlying model, and that improvements to Legora's harness raised output quality by approximately 5%.
pts.d: Legora attributes a relative quality increase between June and July 2026 to harness and platform changes while holding the model set constant. The authors further claim that continuous benchmarking identifies improvements that translate into a better product and greater customer value. The stated gain concerns benchmark output quality, not lawyer productivity, legal outcomes or cost savings.

pts.k: The authors report that model choice matters more for longer, more complex legal tasks and involves trade-offs among quality, speed and cost.
pts.d: Within Legora's benchmark, the authors report similar performance on short work but greater variation as complexity increases. They identify Fable 5, Grok 4.5, Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 as outperforming the average on the longest tasks. They describe Grok 4.5 as having the lowest time per case with high output quality, and Grok 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8 as offering high quality at below-average cost. They qualify the importance of quality rankings by noting that speed and cost may be more important for repetitive or bulk tasks.

pts.k: The authors claim that source transparency is necessary for trust in AI legal analysis and enables lawyers to fact-check its outputs.
pts.d: Legora says its answers must carry citations and reports differences between models in citation coverage and coverage of consulted sources. OpenAI models are described as ranking highest on Cited Answers, while Fable 5 and Opus 4.8 are described as particularly strong on Grounding. As defined in the source, these measures concern citation presence and whether consulted documents are cited; they are not reported hallucination rates or measurements of completed human verification.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rely primarily on Legora's own benchmark, using partner-supplied legal workflows, expert-written rubrics and automated judging inside its production-equivalent environment.
pts.d: The authors report a full evaluation corpus of 5,161 cases and 11,075 source documents across 28 practice areas, with each case reviewed by a legal professional. BAR itself is a selected subset of hundreds of cases drafted by law-firm partners and Legora's legal engineers. Each case is run three times and scored by an LLM judge against binary criteria weighted by importance. Quality, latency, public-list-price cost and citation measures support the comparative findings. A same-model June–July comparison supports the harness-improvement claim. The supplied charts provide relative measures rather than underlying numeric series; the authors do not supply absolute completion rates, measured human time savings or independent replication of the performance findings. AfterQuery's stated review concerns the methodology illustrated by one synthetic case, not independent validation of all reported results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe performance as of July 2026 within Legora's harness, with an explicitly dated June–July improvement and ongoing rather than dated forecasts of further progress.
pts.d: The page was updated on 28 July 2026. Its model comparisons apply to the tested models running the same cases through Legora's system, with access restricted to the case environment. Cases use synthesized and/or anonymized partner data and generally remain private; the authors argue that this protects intellectual property and prevents benchmark familiarity from inflating scores. The difficulty categories represent a few hours to half a day, one to three days, and a week or more up to hundreds of hours of senior-associate effort. The authors promise continuing corpus growth and a technical follow-up, but provide no timetable for autonomous legal practice or workforce substitution.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern legal teams using Legora, lawyers handling increasingly complex matters, and the engineers and model labs improving the system.
pts.d: Law-firm and other legal-team users are presented as beneficiaries of better deliverables, model selection informed by quality–cost–speed trade-offs, and citations that support human checking. Senior associates provide the reference point for task scope; the source does not predict reductions in their numbers or changes to promotion structures. Legora's legal engineers and partner lawyers design and weight evaluation cases, while model labs receive feedback to improve legal performance. The source makes no concrete claims about law-firm pricing changes, ALSP market share, access to justice or employment displacement.
